items.title: Kidd Jordan interviewed by Monk Rowe, Rome, New York, August 24, 2006
items.q: when I studied Bird and saw where Bird, when I finally learned how chords was when I was young and finally did Bird... Bird got some other kind of secrets.

ctx.x: Before I leave this, there was two things I wanted to point out. One that your bass player said, he says if you had an improviser who didn’t really have a tone or a sound then this would fail. You have to be familiar with silence and all kinds of sounds to carry this out. He’s saying that to play this kind of music you’ve got to have some juice to your sound already. In other words you were talking about you’ve got to be able to play your instrument first. That just playing free is not an excuse for lack of…

Oh that’s right, that’s right exactly. And it’s not an excuse for not being able to hear. See that’s, when they first started in New York especially, everybody would be going on the stand and trying, twenty or fifteen people just running on and on and over. But when it boiled down and later on as the music kept developing all of those stopped coming on the stand. I mean it started getting to the point where people knew you got to hear in order to know what you’re doing, I don’t care how out it is. And there’s a…

what I alluded to at the beginning. You’ve got to know how you work, how you are inside and how you work in opposed to how the other people do some things. And like sometimes a guy says, “man you’re not playing the changes.” I say, “I might not be playing the changes but I’m playing the sound of the song.
